PLA's high stiffness (elastic modulus around 3.0-3.5 GPa, noticeably higher than PETG's ~2.0-2.2 GPa or ABS's ~1.8-2.2 GPa) means a PLA part resists deforming under load in the first place — for many glancing or moderate hits, the part simply doesn't move enough to reach its (admittedly lower) breaking strain. Ductility only becomes the deciding factor once a hit is hard enough to actually strain the material significantly, and a stiffer part reaches that threshold at a higher force than a more flexible one of the same wall thickness.

**Print quality dominates real-world toughness more than material choice.** PLA is, by a wide margin, the easiest filament to get consistent, well-adhered layers from on inexpensive, unmodified printers — no enclosure, no heated chamber, minimal warping, forgiving of imperfect cooling and retraction settings. A cracked or delaminated part almost always fails at a layer line or a print defect (a void, poor first-layer adhesion, insufficient wall count) rather than through bulk material fracture, so a material that prints reliably well produces tougher real parts in practice than a "tougher" material printed poorly. Nylon and ABS have better bulk material properties but are meaningfully harder to print defect-free without a proper enclosure and drying setup that many hobbyists don't have.

**Cost enables thickness, and thickness is the real armor budget lever.** PLA/PLA+ is inexpensive enough (roughly $20-25/kg, same ballpark as PETG/ABS) that builders default to thick walls and moderate-to-high infill (2.5-4mm walls, 40-60%+ infill) rather than thin shells — and because weight-per-area scales with thickness regardless of which plastic is used, the practical comparison in a real build is often "thick PLA" versus "thin nylon" rather than equal-thickness PLA versus nylon, and thick-but-more-brittle frequently outperforms thin-but-tougher in this class.

**Disposability is a feature.** Because reprinting a cracked PLA shell is cheap and fast (often overnight, for a few dollars of filament), plastic-antweight competitors can treat armor as consumable — expecting to reprint a shell between fights rather than requiring one panel to survive an entire tournament undamaged. This changes the optimization target from "never crack" to "crack in a way that's easy and cheap to replace," which favors PLA's low cost and print ease over a pricier, harder-to-print material that might survive marginally more hits before failing.

**PLA+ specifically** is a modified PLA blend (formulations vary by brand) that trades a small amount of PLA's stiffness for meaningfully better impact resistance and elongation, narrowing the toughness gap with PETG somewhat while keeping most of standard PLA's easy-printing behavior — many competitive plastic-antweight builders default to PLA+ over standard PLA specifically for this reason when the two cost about the same.

chunks.title: Carbon/Glass-Filled Filament: Stiffness vs Brittleness and Nozzle Wear
chunks.body_md:
Short-fiber-reinforced filaments — chopped carbon fiber or glass fiber blended into a PLA, PETG, or nylon base — are marketed heavily on their stiffness gains, and the numbers are real: a carbon-fiber-reinforced part can be roughly 200-500% stiffer (higher elastic modulus) than the same part printed in the unfilled base polymer, because the short, stiff fibers carry load very efficiently along their length wherever they happen to be oriented by the print path. For parts that need to resist bending or sagging under a steady load — long weapon-motor mount arms, frame spines, anything acting like a beam — that stiffness gain is genuinely valuable and can eliminate flex that would otherwise misalign a weapon or drivetrain.

**The tensile strength gain is much smaller than the stiffness gain, and that gap misleads people.** While elastic modulus jumps dramatically, actual tensile strength typically increases only 20-100% over the base polymer in the strongest print orientation, and can be flat or even lower in other orientations, because the reinforcement's benefit depends heavily on fiber alignment relative to the load and on how well the fiber-matrix interface holds together. Builders sometimes see "carbon fiber" on a spec sheet and assume a proportional jump in overall strength and impact resistance, when the real gain is concentrated almost entirely in stiffness, not toughness.

**Brittleness is the real hidden cost.** Every embedded fiber end is a stress concentrator, and the interface between a stiff fiber and the surrounding (relatively soft) polymer matrix is a mechanically weak plane where a crack can initiate and run. The practical result is that CF/GF-filled parts are noticeably more brittle than their unfilled base polymer — they resist bending better right up until they don't, and then they tend to crack or snap rather than deform, which is close to the opposite of what you want from a direct-impact armor face. This is why fiber-filled filament is a good choice for a stiff internal frame rail or a weapon-support arm set back from the impact zone, and a poor choice for the outer panel that actually takes a hit — an unfilled base polymer, or better yet a TPU skin, will typically survive a direct impact better than the "stronger-sounding" fiber-filled version at the same wall thickness.

**Nozzle wear is a real, recurring cost.** Chopped fibers are abrasive enough to wear out a standard brass nozzle's orifice within roughly a few hundred grams to a kilogram of printing, progressively widening the hole and degrading extrusion consistency and dimensional accuracy well before the wear becomes visually obvious. Printing any meaningful volume of CF/GF filament essentially requires switching to a hardened steel or ruby-tipped nozzle, which adds cost and, for ruby nozzles particularly, some fragility of its own (they can crack if dropped or over-tightened). Builders who print occasional small CF-reinforced parts on an otherwise-brass-nozzle printer often accept the nozzle wear as a cost of doing business; builders printing CF-filled parts regularly generally dedicate a hardened-nozzle setup to it.

chunks.title: Why Acrylic Is a Trap for Combat Robot Armor
chunks.body_md:
Acrylic (PMMA, often sold as Plexiglas) is one of the most common beginner mistakes in combat robot armor selection, and the reason is entirely predictable once you understand why: its datasheet numbers look competitive with genuinely good armor plastics, but the specific number that actually predicts impact survival tells the opposite story.

**The trap, precisely:** acrylic's tensile strength (roughly 70 MPa) and stiffness (elastic modulus around 3.0-3.3 GPa) look comparable to, or even better than, tougher plastics like nylon or polycarbonate on a spec sheet a beginner might glance at while comparison-shopping. What that comparison misses is elongation-to-break — the percentage a material can stretch before it fractures — where acrylic manages only about 3-5%, versus polycarbonate's 100%+ or nylon's 60-100%+. Tensile strength measured in a slow, steady pull test says almost nothing about how a material behaves under the very fast, very high-force loading of a weapon impact; that behavior is governed by toughness and ductility, and acrylic has essentially none of either. It has almost no capacity to yield plastically and absorb energy — when the load exceeds its strength, it doesn't bend or dent, it fractures immediately and completely.

**Why it shatters instead of dents:** acrylic is a fully amorphous, highly cross-linked-feeling (though not actually cross-linked) rigid polymer with very limited chain mobility at room temperature, so unlike polyethylene or polycarbonate, its molecular structure offers no mechanism to absorb impact energy through chain slippage or reorientation before a crack initiates. Once a crack starts — often at a machining mark, a laser-cut edge, or simply the point of impact — it propagates through the brittle material almost instantly, which is why acrylic shatters into multiple sharp-edged shards rather than cracking in one place and staying together.

**Laser cutting makes it worse, and laser cutting is exactly how most hobbyists cut it.** Acrylic is one of the easiest and most popular materials to laser-cut, which is part of its appeal to beginners with access to a laser cutter or cutting service. But the laser-cut edge leaves micro-fractures and localized heat-affected embrittlement right along the cut line — precisely the geometry (an edge, likely also load-bearing in a bolted panel) most likely to see stress during an impact, compounding acrylic's already-poor impact toughness.

**Safety, not just performance:** beyond simply failing to protect the robot's internals, a shattering acrylic panel sends sharp plastic shards into the arena, which is a real safety concern for the robot itself, its opponent, and anyone nearby — this is why most build guides and community wikis explicitly warn against acrylic as an armor material, not just as suboptimal but as actively unsuitable.

**What to use instead for the same cost:** PETG or PLA sheet/printed parts cost roughly the same as acrylic sheet per kg and offer dramatically better elongation-to-break and impact toughness; polycarbonate costs a bit more but offers far superior impact resistance (with its own notch-sensitivity caveats). There is essentially no combat-robot armor scenario where acrylic is the correct choice over these alternatives at a comparable price point.

chunks.title: Tungsten Ballast and Precision Weight Budgeting
chunks.body_md:
Hitting a 1 lb (453.6g) weight limit exactly, without going over, is a routine late-build problem: a finished antweight almost never lands precisely on the limit, and builders either need to shave grams off a too-heavy design or add grams to a too-light one to use the full weight allowance competitively. Tungsten (or tungsten-heavy-alloy) ballast solves the "too light" side of that problem better than any other practical material because of one number: density.

**Why density is the whole point.** Tungsten heavy alloy (typically 90-97% tungsten with a nickel-iron or nickel-copper binder) has a density around 17-18.5 g/cm³ — roughly 2.2-2.3 times denser than steel and about 4x denser than titanium. That means a given amount of added mass takes up the smallest possible volume of any practical ballast material, which matters enormously in a 1 lb robot where internal space is at an absolute premium. Adding 20g of steel ballast requires roughly 2.5cm³ of space; the same 20g in tungsten heavy alloy takes about 1.1-1.2cm³ — often the difference between ballast fitting in a design's remaining internal void or not fitting at all.

**Two distinct uses:** (1) **Fine weight-limit tuning** — a small tungsten cube, disc, or moldable tungsten-loaded putty pressed into a cavity near the end of the build to bring total weight up to just under 453.6g, squeezing every gram of performance out of the weight allowance rather than leaving unused margin on the table (unused weight margin is performance left on the table — that gram could have gone to a bigger battery, thicker armor, or a heavier weapon). (2) **Weapon rim/moment-of-inertia loading** — packing tungsten inserts into the rim of a spinner disc or drum increases the weapon's moment of inertia (and therefore its stored kinetic energy at a given RPM, since KE scales with moment of inertia) without increasing the weapon's outer diameter, which would otherwise risk a rules or clearance violation. This is a targeted way to make a spinner weapon hit harder without redesigning its shape.

**Cost and handling considerations.** Tungsten heavy alloy costs considerably more per kg than steel ballast (commonly in the tens of dollars per pound range for small hobby quantities), which is a real but usually acceptable premium given how little total ballast mass a 1 lb robot typically needs (often just 5-30g). It is non-toxic (unlike lead, which some events restrict or discourage for exactly that reason) and machines similarly to a hard steel with carbide tooling, though pure unalloyed tungsten is considerably more brittle and harder to machine cleanly than the heavy-alloy composite grades typically sold for ballast use.

**Not a structural or armor material.** Despite its impressive density, tungsten ballast should not be mistaken for an armor upgrade — its role is purely mass placement, tucked into a cavity or rim where its weight helps but its (mediocre, for a metal) toughness is never tested by a direct hit.

chunks.title: Elastomers and Deliberate Compliance in Antweight Design
chunks.body_md:
Not every material decision in a combat robot is about maximizing hardness or strength — a significant category of material choices is about deliberately adding softness (compliance) exactly where a rigid connection would otherwise transmit damaging shock into something fragile. Elastomers (silicone, polyurethane, foam, and rubber grommets) are the tools for this job, and understanding where and why they're used rounds out a complete antweight materials picture.

**The problem compliance solves:** a weapon impact delivers a very sudden deceleration/acceleration pulse to the whole chassis. A component rigidly bolted to that chassis — a receiver, an ESC, a flight controller, a battery — experiences that same sudden shock, and solder joints, connector pins, and battery internals are often the weakest link in the entire robot, failing from shock even when the armor and structure survive the hit completely intact. This is a very common and often misdiagnosed cause of "the bot just died" after a hit that didn't visibly damage the shell.

**Silicone rubber** is used mainly for small vibration-isolating mounts, grommets, and wire management around electronics. Its main strengths are an extremely wide temperature range and good compliance; its main weakness is relatively low tear/abrasion resistance, which is fine for a lightly-loaded grommet but not for something that sees repeated mechanical wear.

**Cast polyurethane elastomer** covers a wider durometer range and has better abrasion/tear resistance than silicone, making it the more common choice for anything that sees repeated mechanical contact rather than just isolating vibration — drive wheel tires (durometer chosen to balance traction against wear), flexible wedge lips that need to bend under contact with the floor or an opponent's underside, and shock-absorbing bumper pads.

**Foam padding** (EVA or closed-cell polyurethane) is the internal, lightweight option — wedged around a battery or behind a PCB to break the direct shock path from a rigid mount into a fragile component. It adds negligible weight (foam density is roughly 1/8 to 1/10 that of solid plastics) and costs very little, making it one of the best weight-to-reliability trades available; the tradeoff is that foam isn't structural in any sense and can compress/lose effectiveness after many hits.

**Rubber grommets and standoff mounts** apply the same shock-isolation principle at fastener points — swapping a rigid metal standoff for a rubber-grommeted one under a receiver or ESC costs almost nothing in weight or money but meaningfully reduces the chance that a hard hit which the armor survives fine still kills the electronics through shock alone.

**The general design principle:** wherever a rigid, direct mechanical path exists between the point of impact and a fragile component, a small amount of engineered compliance — the right elastomer, at the right durometer, in the right place — interrupts that path and converts a damaging shock into a manageable one. This is a deliberate, low-cost design choice available at almost every point in a 1 lb build, not just an armor problem.

chunks.title: 3D-Printed Material Selection for Plastic Antweights: Overview
chunks.body_md:
Plastic-antweight is defined by its reliance on hobby FDM 3D printing for structure and armor, which makes filament selection the single biggest set of material decisions in the class. Here's how the common options stack up against each other for a builder deciding what to load into the printer next.

**PLA/PLA+** remains the default starting point and, for many competitive builders, the default finishing point too — see the dedicated PLA dominance discussion for the full reasoning, but in short: cheapest, easiest to print reliably, stiffest of the common options, and cheap enough to treat as disposable/reprintable between fights.

**PETG** is the most common upgrade path when a builder wants more ductility/toughness than PLA without taking on ABS's warping problems or nylon's moisture sensitivity — it's the "more forgiving toughness" option, at some cost in stiffness and print cleanliness (stringing).

**ABS/ASA** earns its place mainly through heat resistance (useful for parts mounted near a hot weapon motor or ESC) and, for ASA specifically, UV/weather resistance — not generally chosen for extra impact toughness over PETG, and it demands more printer setup (heated bed, ideally an enclosure) to avoid warping and weak inter-layer bonds.

**Nylon (PA6/PA12)** offers the best all-round bulk toughness and fatigue resistance of the common printables — excellent for living hinges, gears, and high-flex mounts — but its strong hygroscopicity (it absorbs moisture from ambient air within hours and prints poorly wet) and warping tendency make it less common than PLA/PETG for full armor shells; it shows up more in mechanisms than outer panels. **PA-CF** (carbon-fiber-reinforced nylon) pushes stiffness and dry strength even higher for structural, non-impact-facing parts, at the cost of added brittleness and serious nozzle wear.

**PC filament** offers the highest strength/heat-resistance ceiling of common printables but requires high-temperature, typically enclosed printing setups that exclude a lot of hobby-grade machines, so it's a premium/advanced option rather than a mainstream choice.

**PP (polypropylene)** is the lightest common filament and has outstanding fatigue resistance for living-hinge features, but its notoriously poor bed adhesion makes it hard to print reliably, restricting it to small flexible features (snap latches, hinges) rather than structural or armor use.

**TPU (95A/85A/60D)** is the outlier on this list because it isn't rigid at all — it's the compliant, energy-absorbing skin material discussed in depth elsewhere, used over a rigid frame from one of the materials above rather than as a replacement for one.

**Carbon/glass-filled variants** of PLA, PETG, or nylon trade toughness for stiffness and are best reserved for structural members set back from direct impact (frame rails, weapon-motor mount arms) rather than the outer armor face itself.

**A practical build recipe many competitive plastic-antweights converge on:** a PLA+ or PETG structural shell for stiffness and mounting rigidity, at generous wall thickness (2.5-4mm) and moderate-to-high infill, wrapped or capped with a TPU 95A compliant skin at the highest-impact-risk faces, with small PA6/nylon parts for hinges/latches that need to flex repeatedly, and PA-CF or plain filament used sparingly for load-bearing internal ribs where stiffness matters more than impact resistance.
